oneSentence: A machine learning method that assigns one or more predefined category labels to an input based on learned patterns.
plainExplanation:
Classification is used when you want a system to choose one or more categories from a fixed set. For example, an email might be labelled “spam” or “not spam”, or a document might be labelled “invoice”, “contract” or “report”. The input can be text, an image, a sound clip or a row of numbers.

During training, the system is shown many examples along with the correct category or categories. Those correct categories are called labels. From these examples, it adjusts internal settings so that certain patterns in the input become linked with certain labels.

Later, during inference, a new input goes in. The system turns that input into measurable signals, often called features, such as words present in a message or shapes in an image. It then produces a prediction: which class or classes apply, sometimes with a score for each class.

Classification is different from regression, which predicts a number such as temperature or price. It is also different from clustering, which groups similar items without using pre-named categories. In classification, the categories are defined in advance, even if the model sometimes gets them wrong.

everydayAnalogy.title: Sorting buttons into labelled trays
everydayAnalogy.story: Sam is shown many buttons already placed in trays labelled “red”, “blue”, “two-hole” and “four-hole”. From those examples, Sam learns which visible features correspond to each label. For a new button, Sam checks its colour and number of holes, then places it in the matching trays. If only colour labels are allowed, it receives one label. If colour and hole-count labels may both apply, it receives more than one.

everydayAnalogy.limitation: A person tuning a radio can use broad real-world knowledge and can change the categories if needed. A classifier usually works only with the classes it was trained for, and its internal matching process is mathematical rather than conscious listening. Also, many classifiers output scores for all classes at once, not a person-like step-by-step judgement.

visual.title: How classification turns an input into a category
visual.learningObjective: After viewing this, the reader should be able to say that classification takes an input, measures useful features, compares learned patterns and outputs one named class.
visual.description: A left-to-right flow diagram with four boxes connected by arrows. It shows a new input entering the system, being converted into features, compared with patterns learned during training, and ending with a class prediction and confidence scores. Read from left to right.

steps.label: 1. New input arrives
steps.explanation: A text, image, sound clip or data record is presented to the model for sorting.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a box on the left labelled “Input” with small icons for a document, photo and waveform. Add a caption: “Example: message, image or form entry”.

steps.label: 2. Signals are measured
steps.explanation: The system represents parts of the input as features, such as words, shapes, colours or numeric values.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a second box labelled “Features” containing tokens like “urgent”, “invoice”, a small shape outline and bars for numeric values.

steps.label: 3. Learned patterns are compared
steps.explanation: The model uses patterns learned from labelled examples to estimate how strongly the input matches each class.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a third box labelled “Model” with three horizontal score bars named Class A, Class B and Class C, each at different lengths.

steps.label: 4. A class is returned
steps.explanation: The output is a prediction, often the highest-scoring class, sometimes alongside confidence-like scores.
steps.visualInstruction: Draw a final box labelled “Prediction” with one highlighted result such as “Invoice” and smaller secondary scores beneath it.

visual.interaction: Hovering or tapping each box reveals one concrete example for text, image and tabular data; arrows highlight in sequence from input to prediction.
visual.accessibilityDescription: The diagram is a four-step flow from left to right. First, a new input enters, such as a message, image or form entry. Second, the system measures features from that input, like words, shapes or numbers. Third, the model compares those features with patterns learned earlier from labelled examples and produces scores for each possible class. Fourth, it returns the class with the strongest score, for example labelling a document as an invoice. The main lesson is that classification outputs a named category, not an open-ended answer or a numeric estimate.
visual.reducedMotionDescription: A static left-to-right diagram with four labelled boxes: Input, Features, Model and Prediction. Short example text under each box replaces any animated highlighting.

workedExample.scenario: Classifying a facilities ticket before the duty officer hands over the service desk at a Geneva duty station.
workedExample.input: Ticket text: “The meeting room on level 3 is too warm, and the wall control does not respond.”
process: The classifier receives the ticket text as input.
It identifies features associated with the available labels, including “too warm”, “wall control” and “does not respond”.
It compares those features with patterns learned from tickets previously labelled “temperature issue”, “equipment fault” or “access issue”.
It calculates a score for each label: temperature issue 0.94, equipment fault 0.72 and access issue 0.04.
Because this is a multilabel classifier, it returns every label above the set threshold of 0.50.
workedExample.result: Predicted labels: “temperature issue” and “equipment fault”. The ticket can be routed to facilities maintenance, with the duty officer able to correct the labels if the request has been misread.

unWorkplaceExample.scenario: Late in the afternoon, a budget officer in a country office is reviewing applications for a finance roster before the proposed shortlist goes to the front office at close of business. An approved screening tool classifies each application as “profile matched”, “manual review” or “required criterion not evidenced”, using patterns learned from previously labelled applications.
unWorkplaceExample.relevance: Classification determines which predefined label each application receives. The budget officer needs to examine how the training labels were assigned, what evidence drives each category, how borderline cases are handled and whether errors fall unevenly across groups. The output is a triage label, not a recruitment decision.
unWorkplaceExample.caution: Applications contain personal and potentially sensitive HR information. They must not be uploaded to an external or unapproved tool. A classifier must not make or effectively determine the shortlist: every exclusion requires meaningful human review, since biased training labels or missed evidence could unfairly affect a candidate.

whyItMatters: Classification affects how information is routed, filtered and prioritised. A system may flag content as risky, sort messages into queues, or label documents for faster handling. If you understand classification, you can ask practical questions: What are the classes? Who chose the labels? How often does it confuse one class with another? What happens when it is unsure? These questions matter because errors have consequences. A false alarm can waste time or unfairly block something. A missed case can hide an urgent issue. Non-specialists do not need to build classifiers, but they often need to judge whether one is suitable, what data it needs and where human review is still necessary.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Classification always gives a yes-or-no answer.
commonMisconceptions.correction: Some classifiers are binary, with two classes such as approved or rejected, but many choose among three or more classes. A system can also return a score for each class, not just a single hard label.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: If the model is 90% confident, it is correct 90% of the time for every case.
commonMisconceptions.correction: A score is not automatically a trustworthy probability. Some models are poorly calibrated, meaning their confidence-like numbers do not match real-world accuracy. Performance can also differ across classes and contexts.

commonMisconceptions.misconception: Classification finds natural groups in data by itself.
commonMisconceptions.correction: That describes clustering more than classification. In classification, the categories are named in advance and the system learns from examples linked to those labels.

simpleVsTechnical.simple: Classification is teaching a system to put each new item into one or more named buckets, like sorting messages into “spam” or “not spam”.
simpleVsTechnical.technical: In machine learning, classification is a supervised learning task that maps an input x to one or more labels from a finite set of classes. A model is trained on labelled examples to learn a decision function or class score based on features in the input. At inference time, it computes scores for the possible classes and returns one or more labels, depending on the design. Common variants include binary classification, multiclass classification and multilabel classification, where one item can receive more than one label. Evaluation often examines per-class performance, confusion between classes and trade-offs such as false positives versus false negatives.

keyTakeaway: Classification uses patterns learned from labelled examples to assign one or more predefined categories to a new input. A score supports the prediction, but is not proof that the label is correct.

quickCheck.question: Which situation is a classification task?
options: Grouping unlabeled photos by visual similarity
Writing a summary of a meeting note
quickCheck.explanation: Classification chooses from predefined categories. “Urgent”, “routine” and “irrelevant” are named classes decided in advance. Predicting rainfall is regression, grouping unlabeled photos is clustering, and writing a summary is a text generation task.

issues.problem: These fields define classification as assigning exactly one category. That excludes multilabel classification, which the page later identifies as a classification variant. The definition and takeaway therefore contradict the technical explanation.
issues.fix: State that classification can assign one or more predefined category labels. In the plain explanation, refer to the class or classes that apply.

issues.problem: The simple text says every item goes into one bucket. The technical text initially says classification maps an input to one label, then says multilabel classification can assign more than one label. This is an internal contradiction.
issues.fix: Use “one or more” in both descriptions, and say that inference returns one or more labels depending on the design.

issues.problem: The learning objective and accessibility description present returning one class as a property of classification in general. The diagram actually describes single-label classification and contradicts the page's inclusion of multilabel classification.
issues.fix: Change the title to “Single-label classification assigns an input to a category”. In the learning objective, replace “classification” with “single-label classification”. In the final accessibility sentence, replace “classification outputs one named category” with “single-label classification outputs a named category”.
